items.title: The parabolic Hecke module and the antispherical standard basis
items.statement:
Work with the normalized type-$A$ Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over
$A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ of
[[def-normalized-type-a-hecke-algebra-and-its-bar-involution]]: generators
$H_s$ with $H_s^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_s$, standard basis $\{H_w:w\in S_n\}$, bar
involution $\overline{H_s}=H_s^{-1}=H_s-(v^{-1}-v)$ and Kazhdan--Lusztig basis
$\{\underline H_w\}$ of
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]], so that
$\underline H_s=H_s+v$. The underlying Coxeter data are those of
[[def-symmetric-group]], [[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]] and
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]].

Fix $J\subseteq S=\{s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\}$, let $W_J=\langle s:s\in J\rangle\subseteq S_n$
be the standard parabolic subgroup and let
$\Phi_J=\Phi\cap\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{\alpha_s:s\in J\}$ be its
standard type-$A$ root subsystem, all in the conventions of
[[def-cg-parabolic-quotient-and-two-sided-minima]].

**The two characters.** Let $H_J\subseteq H_v(n)$ be the subalgebra generated
by $\{H_s:s\in J\}$. For $s\in J$ the quadratic relation makes $v^{-1}$ and
$-v$ the two roots of $x^2-(v^{-1}-v)x-1=0$, so there are well-defined algebra
homomorphisms $\varphi_+,\varphi_-:H_J\to A$ with

$$\varphi_+(H_s)=v^{-1},\qquad \varphi_-(H_s)=-v\qquad(s\in J).$$

Viewing $A$ through $\varphi_+$ (resp. $\varphi_-$) as a right $H_J$-module
gives the **spherical parabolic module** $M^J:=A\otimes_{H_J}H_v(n)$ and the
**antispherical parabolic module** $N^J:=A\otimes_{H_J}H_v(n)$, right
$H_v(n)$-modules under right multiplication on the second factor.

**Coset representatives.** Throughout, $\Phi^+$ is the positive system of
$\Phi$ and $\Phi_J^+=\Phi_J\cap\Phi^+$, and

$${}^JW:=\{w\in S_n:\ell(sw)>\ell(w)\ \text{for all }s\in J\},\qquad W^J:=\{w\in S_n:\ell(ws)>\ell(w)\ \text{for all }s\in J\}$$

are the left-minimal and right-minimal representatives of the cosets
$W_Jw$ and $wW_J$, respectively. By
[[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] and
[[thm-cg-parabolic-intersections-and-coset-factorization]] every $w\in S_n$
factors uniquely as $w=l y$ with $l\in W_J$, $y\in{}^JW$ and
$\ell(w)=\ell(l)+\ell(y)$, and inversion interchanges ${}^JW$ and $W^J$.

The definitions of $\varphi_\pm$ use only the quadratic relation on generators;
no further module-theoretic input enters.
items.strategy: Conventions and well-definedness only. The signs $v^{-1},-v$ solve $t^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)t$ by direct expansion ([[def-normalized-type-a-hecke-algebra-and-its-bar-involution]]), so $\varphi_\pm$ are algebra maps because the Hecke relations in a single factor are generated by the quadratic relations together with the braid relations, on which scalars act trivially. The coset statements are the standard parabolic factorization of [[thm-cg-parabolic-intersections-and-coset-factorization]] and [[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]]; inversion preserves length and interchanges left and right descents, so ${^JW}^{-1}=W^J$. The bases $\{1\otimes H_x:x\in{^JW}\}$ and the right action formulas are asserted nowhere here: they are the content of [[lem-the-parabolic-hecke-modules-have-standard-bases-actions-and-compatible-bars]]. The spherical module is recorded because the singular-block multiplicities are read in the spherical normalization; the antispherical module is recorded because its canonical basis is the induced-sign analogue and its coefficients differ in general.

items.title: The singular integral block and its dot stabilizer
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
published block theory. Work in category $\mathcal O$ of a finite-dimensional
complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ with Cartan $\mathfrak h$,
positive system $\Phi^+$, simple roots $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$, Weyl group
$W$, Weyl vector $\rho$ and dot action $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$, as
in [[def-bgg-category-o]] and
[[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]].

**(1) Dot-antidominant integral weights.** A weight $\mu$ is **dot-antidominant**
if $\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\le0$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi^+$, and
**integral** if $\langle\mu,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z$ for all $i$
([[def-integral-weyl-group-of-a-weight]],
[[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]).

**(2) The dot stabilizer.** Fix such a weight $\mu$ and put
$$J=J(\mu):=\{i:\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle=0\},\qquad W_\mu:=W_J=\langle s_i:i\in J\rangle.$$
Then the dot stabilizer $\{v\in W:v\cdot\mu=\mu\}$ equals $W_J$. Indeed, for
$i\in J$ the reflection $s_i$ fixes $\mu+\rho$, so $W_J$ lies in the
stabilizer; conversely the stabilizer of an integral dot-antidominant weight
is generated by the reflections it contains and is a standard parabolic
([[lem-finite-weyl-closed-chambers-and-stabilizers]], applied to the dominant
vector $-\mu-\rho$), and by
[[def-cg-parabolic-quotient-and-two-sided-minima]] a standard parabolic
subgroup is $W_I$ for the set $I$ of simple reflections it contains, which is
exactly $J$. In particular $w'\cdot\mu=w\cdot\mu$ if and only if
$w^{-1}w'\in W_J$, that is, $w'\in wW_J$.

**(3) The singular integral block.** The **singular integral block**
$\mathcal O_\mu$ is the block of
[[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]] of the central
character $\chi_\mu$ of $\mu$; by
[[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]] two central characters agree
exactly when the highest weights lie in one dot orbit, and by
[[thm-category-o-decomposes-by-generalized-central-character]] the block is a
summand of $\mathcal O$. Its simple objects $L(w\cdot\mu)$, standard objects
$\Delta(w\cdot\mu)=M(w\cdot\mu)$, costandard objects $\nabla(w\cdot\mu)$ and
projective covers $P(w\cdot\mu)$ are indexed by $w\in W$
([[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]],
[[def-verma-module]]); by (2) the label $w\cdot\mu$ depends only on the coset
$wW_J$, so the labels can be normalized by the minimal right coset
representatives

$$W^J=\{w\in W:\ell(ws)>\ell(w)\ \text{for all }s\in J\},$$

which are exactly the elements of minimal length in the cosets $wW_J$
([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (3));
inversion carries $W^J$ onto the minimal left coset representatives ${}^JW$,
and the two families are the label sets of the parabolic Hecke modules of
[[def-parabolic-hecke-module-and-antispherical-standard-basis]].

**(4) Highest-weight structure and multiplicities.** The block is a
highest-weight category: it has enough projectives
([[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]), projective covers have finite
Verma flags ([[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]]), the standard
classes and simple classes are bases of the Grothendieck group
([[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]],
[[prop-the-grothendieck-group-of-o-has-simple-and-standard-bases]]), and it
satisfies BGG reciprocity
$$(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))=[M(y\cdot\mu):L(w\cdot\mu)]$$
([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]], [[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]). The
multiplicity matrix is unitriangular for the refinement of the dominance order
on the dot orbit: $(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(w\cdot\mu))=1$, and
$(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))\neq0$ only if $y\cdot\mu\ge w\cdot\mu$
([[cor-projective-standard-labels-lie-above-the-head]]); the ordinary
standard/costandard Hom and $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ vanishing used on this page is
[[lem-standard-costandard-hom-and-ext-vanishing]].

**(5) Regular versus singular.** The block is **regular** when $J=\varnothing$
(the weight lies on no wall) and **singular** when $J\neq\varnothing$; the
singular translation statements of this page use this notation, and
$J=\varnothing$ recovers the regular case. The genuine regular-parabolic
multiplicity statements below have their own separate explicit dominant
regular base and are not consequences of the notation here.
items.strategy: Conventions and inherited structure only. The stabilizer claim uses the standard fact that for an integral dot-antidominant weight the dot stabilizer is the standard parabolic generated by the simple reflections it contains ([[lem-finite-weyl-closed-chambers-and-stabilizers]], applied to the dominant vector -mu-rho); the coset description of the label set is $w'\cdot\mu=w\cdot\mu\iff w^{-1}w'\in W_\mu\iff w'\in wW_J$. The block theory, the index set $W$, the highest-weight structure, the Grothendieck bases and BGG reciprocity are quoted from the published items; no new multiplicity assertion is made here. The normalization by $W^J$ (rather than $W$) is recorded exactly because it matches the minimal coset representatives of the parabolic Hecke modules and the inversion dictionary $W^J={^JW}^{-1}$. The finite singular block inherits enough projective covers and ordinary Verma flags from the actual published items. BGG gives diagonal standard multiplicity1 and only standards above each head. Canonical maximal-weight Verma traces remove higher factors; the remaining labelled Verma quotient has higher-Verma-filtered kernel, giving the highest-weight data. The actual ordinary standard/costandard Hom and Ext1 supplier applies to these ordinary Vermas; this is not the later generalized-Verma restriction. The published Grothendieck-bases theorem supplies the stated simple/standard bases.

items.title: Standard parabolic and Levi subalgebras from a subset of simple roots
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the published root-space/sl2 suppliers. Let g be finite-dimensional complex semisimple with Cartan h, roots Phi, positives Phi^+, simple roots alpha_i, and J a subset of the simple indices. Put Phi_J=Phi intersect span_R{alpha_j:j in J}, H_j=the coroot of alpha_j, h_J=span_C{H_j:j in J} and z_J={h:alpha_j(h)=0 for all j in J}. Define s_J=h_J plus the root spaces of Phi_J, l_J=h plus those root spaces, u_J=the sum of positive root spaces outside Phi_J, and p_J=l_J plus u_J. Then h=h_J direct-sum z_J, s_J is semisimple with roots Phi_J, and l_J=s_J direct-sum z_J is reductive with center z_J, Cartan h and Weyl group W_J. The sums l_J,u_J,p_J are Lie subalgebras, u_J is the nilradical of p_J, and p_J=l_J semidirect u_J is its reductive parabolic Levi decomposition. In the published radical-based sense of def-levi-subalgebra-and-levi-decomposition, rad(p_J)=z_J plus u_J and s_J is the SEMISIMPLE Levi factor complementing that radical; l_J need not be semisimple. The parabolic contains b and equals b plus the negative Phi_J root spaces. For J empty it is b; for J all it is g. There exists zeta in z_J with alpha_i(zeta)=1 outside J, giving u_J strictly positive integral degrees and v_J (the outside negative radical) strictly negative degrees, with l_J degree0. Both radicals have finite-dimensional fixed-degree PBW slices. The construction depends only on the positive system and J.
items.strategy:
Put h_J=span{H_j:j∈J}, z_J={h:α_j(h)=0 for all j∈J}. The finite-type Cartan
principal submatrix is nonsingular because its symmetrized Gram matrix is
positive definite. Thus h=h_J⊕z_J. Set
s_J=h_J⊕⊕_{α∈Φ_J}g_α, l_J=s_J⊕z_J, and
u_J=⊕_{β∈Φ^+\Φ_J^+}g_β, v_J=⊕_{β∈Φ^-\Φ_J^-}g_β.
For alpha in Phi_J its Killing-dual vector, hence its rescaled coroot, lies in h_J by linearity of the Killing dual of the J-root expansion. Thus opposite root brackets lie in h_J. Root brackets make s_J,l_J,u_J,p_J=l_J⊕u_J and v_J Lie subalgebras, with
u_J ideal in p_J and l_J stabilizing u_J and v_J.

The INTRINSIC Killing form of s_J on h_J is Σ_{α∈Φ_J}α(h)α(h'); on the real
coroot span this is positive definite since the roots span its dual. Weight
orthogonality pairs only opposite root spaces; invariance and a root sl2 triple
give K(e_α,f_α)=K(H_α,H_α)/2≠0. Hence this Killing form is nondegenerate,
and the actual Cartan criterion proves s_J semisimple. The centralizer z_J
commutes with s_J, so l_J is reductive and has root system Φ_J and Weyl group W_J.

Choose ζ with α_j(ζ)=0 for j∈J and α_i(ζ)=1 for i∉J. Positive radical roots
have positive integral ζ-degree; negative outside roots have negative degree;
Levi roots have degree0. Thus u_J is nilpotent by its positive grading.
Its nilradical equality requires more than saying l_J is reductive. A nilpotent
ideal I in p_J projects to an ideal of l_J, whose projection into semisimple s_J
is zero. If its remaining image contains nonzero h∈z_J, lift h to x=h+a, a∈u_J.
Some outside simple root has α_i(h)≠0. In the ζ-grading, ad x is upper triangular
with diagonal ad h and has that nonzero eigenvalue. Its corresponding generalized
eigenspace lies in im(ad x)⊂I; hence ad x on I has a nonzero eigenvalue, impossible
for a nilpotent I. So I⊂u_J. Also rad(p_J)=z_J⊕u_J: this is a solvable ideal with
semisimple quotient s_J. Therefore l_J is the REDUCTIVE complement to nilradical,
whereas s_J is the semisimple Levi factor in the published radical-based Definition.
The cases J=empty and J=all have s_J=0 or u_J=v_J=0 as appropriate.

items.title: Standard bases, right actions and bar involutions on the parabolic Hecke modules
items.statement:
Retain the notation of
[[def-parabolic-hecke-module-and-antispherical-standard-basis]] and put
$m_x:=1\otimes H_x$, $n_x:=1\otimes H_x$ for $x\in{}^JW$, and
$C_s:=\underline H_s=H_s+v$ for $s\in S$. Then:

**(1) (Bases.)** The sets $\{m_x:x\in{}^JW\}$ and $\{n_x:x\in{}^JW\}$ are
$A$-bases of $M^J$ and $N^J$ respectively. Indeed every $w\in S_n$ factors
uniquely as $w=ly$ with $l\in W_J$, $y\in{}^JW$, length-additively, and
$\varphi_+(H_l)=v^{-\ell(l)}$ and $\varphi_-(H_l)=(-v)^{\ell(l)}$
are units of $A$, so $1\otimes H_w=\varphi_\pm(H_l)\,(1\otimes H_y)$ in both
modules.

**(2) (Right action.)** For $s\in S$ and $x\in{}^JW$,
$$m_x C_s=\begin{cases}m_{xs}+v\,m_x,&xs\in{}^JW,\ xs>x,\\ m_{xs}+v^{-1}m_x,&xs\in{}^JW,\ xs<x,\\ (v+v^{-1})m_x,&xs\notin{}^JW,\end{cases}\qquad n_xC_s=\begin{cases}n_{xs}+v\,n_x,&xs\in{}^JW,\ xs>x,\\ n_{xs}+v^{-1}n_x,&xs\in{}^JW,\ xs<x,\\ 0,&xs\notin{}^JW.\end{cases}$$

**(3) (Bar.)** The assignment $a\otimes h\mapsto \bar a\otimes\bar h$ (bar on
$A$ and the bar involution of $H_v(n)$) descends to $A$-antilinear
involutions of $M^J$ and $N^J$ that satisfy
$\overline{X\cdot h}=\overline X\cdot\bar h$ and
$$\overline{m_x}=m_x+\sum_{y<x}a_{y,x}m_y,\qquad \overline{n_x}=n_x+\sum_{y<x}b_{y,x}n_y$$
with $a_{y,x},b_{y,x}\in A$ and top coefficient
$a_{x,x}=b_{x,x}=1$.

**(4) (Parabolic property.)** If $x\in{}^JW$ and $s\in S$ with
$xs\notin{}^JW$, then $xs=rx$ for a unique simple $r\in J$ and $xs>x$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct: exhibit the free left $H_J$-basis, compute the right action from the standard multiplication rules, prove the parabolic property from the type-$A$ block criterion, and expand bar along subwords.

1.1 **The bases.** The $A$-span of $\{H_u:u\in W_J\}$ is exactly $H_J$: it contains the generators and is closed under their left and right multiplication by the quadratic multiplication rule, while every $H_u$ is a reduced product of generators in $J$. By [F1], the standard basis partitions as $\{H_uH_y:u\in W_J,\ y\in{}^JW\}$. Hence multiplication is an isomorphism of left $H_J$-modules $\bigoplus_{y\in{}^JW}H_J\to H_v(n)$, $(h_y)_y\mapsto\sum_yh_yH_y$: expanding each $h_y$ in the independent $H_u$ proves injectivity and the unique factorization proves surjectivity. Tensoring this isomorphism with either character module $A$ gives $A\otimes_{H_J}H_v(n)\cong\bigoplus_{y\in{}^JW}A$. The images of the coordinate generators are $m_y$, respectively $n_y$, proving both bases. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 **The two minimal branches.** Let $x\in{}^JW$, $s\in S$ and suppose $xs\in{}^JW$. Since $xs=(xsx^{-1})x$ is the left translate of $x$ by a transposition and $\ell(xs)=\ell(x)\pm1$, [F4] shows that $xs>x$ holds exactly when $\ell(xs)=\ell(x)+1$, and $xs<x$ exactly when $\ell(xs)=\ell(x)-1$. If $xs>x$ then [F2] gives $H_xH_s=H_{xs}$, so by step 1.1 and the module structure $m_xC_s=1\otimes(H_{xs}+vH_x)=m_{xs}+v\,m_x$, and likewise $n_xC_s=n_{xs}+v\,n_x$. If $xs<x$ then $H_xH_s=H_{xs}+(v^{-1}-v)H_x$, so $m_xC_s=m_{xs}+(v^{-1}-v)m_x+v\,m_x=m_{xs}+v^{-1}m_x$, and likewise $n_xC_s=n_{xs}+v^{-1}n_x$. [F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 **The parabolic property.** Let $x\in{}^JW$ and $s=s_j$, and suppose $xs\notin{}^JW$; by [F5] $xs$ has a left descent in $J$: some $r\in J$ has $r+1$ to the left of $r$ in $xs$. Since $x\in{}^JW$ has no such descent, while $xs$ differs from $x$ only by the swap of the entries at positions $j$ and $j+1$, the only changed relative order is that of the values $a:=x(j)$, $b:=x(j+1)$, so $\{r,r+1\}=\{a,b\}$. The order $a=r+1$, $b=r$ is excluded because it would already be a left descent of $x$. Hence $a=r$ and $b=r+1$ with $r\in J$; the two permutations $xs$ and $s_rx$ coincide because both are obtained from $x$ by interchanging the values $r$ and $r+1$. Moreover $\ell(s_rx)>\ell(x)$ because $r\in J$ and $x\in{}^JW$, so $\ell(xs)=\ell(x)+1$ and $xs>x$ by [F4](a),(b); thus $H_xH_s=H_{xs}=H_{s_rx}=H_rH_x$ by [F1] and [F2]. Therefore $m_xC_s=1\otimes(H_{xs}+vH_x)=\varphi_+(H_r)m_x+v\,m_x=(v^{-1}+v)m_x$ and $n_xC_s=\varphi_-(H_r)n_x+v\,n_x=(-v+v)n_x=0$. Uniqueness of $r$ holds because $r$ is the value whose swap produces $xs$; this proves (4) and the third branch of (2). [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 **The bar descent.** The map $\beta(a\otimes h):=\bar a\otimes\bar h$ is well defined on $A\otimes_{H_J}H_v(n)$: it suffices to check $\overline{a\varphi_\pm(t)}\otimes\bar h=\bar a\otimes\overline{th}$ for $t=H_s$, $s\in J$, where the left side is $\bar a\,\overline{\varphi_\pm(H_s)}\otimes\bar h$ and the right side is $\bar a\otimes\overline{H_s}\bar h=\bar a\otimes(H_s-(v^{-1}-v))\bar h=\bar a\,\varphi_\pm(H_s-(v^{-1}-v))\otimes\bar h$, and $\varphi_+(H_s-(v^{-1}-v))=v^{-1}+(v-v^{-1})=v=\overline{v^{-1}}$, $\varphi_-(H_s-(v^{-1}-v))=-v+(v-v^{-1})=-v^{-1}=\overline{-v}$ by [F3]; multiplicativity extends this to all $t$. The map is $A$-antilinear, involutive ($\beta^2=\mathrm{id}$ because bar is an involution on $A$ and on $H_v(n)$), and satisfies $\beta(X\cdot h')=\beta(X)\cdot\overline{h'}$ because $(a\otimes h)\cdot h'=a\otimes hh'$ maps to $\bar a\otimes\overline{hh'}=\bar a\otimes\bar h\bar h'=(\bar a\otimes\bar h)\cdot\bar h'$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 **Triangular expansion and top coefficient.** For $x=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$ reduced, [F3] gives $\overline{H_x}=\prod_{m=1}^k(H_{s_{i_m}}-(v^{-1}-v))$. The term choosing every generator is $H_x$. Every other term is a scalar times a product of fewer than $k$ generators selected from this word. Successive use of [F2] expands such a product into $H_z$ whose group labels are products of subwords of the selected word: each multiplication retains the old label or appends the current generator. Deletion of pairs in [F4] reduces each such group word to a reduced subword of the original reduced expression for $x$. Thus $z\le x$, and $\ell(z)<k$ because at most $k-1$ letters were retained, so $z<x$. Consequently $\overline{H_x}=H_x+\sum_{z<x}c_zH_z$. For each $z<x$ factor $z=uy$ length-additively with $u\in W_J$, $y\in{}^JW$. A reduced expression of $z$ contains a reduced suffix for $y$, so $y\le z<x$. In either module $1\otimes H_z=\varphi_\pm(H_u)(1\otimes H_y)$. Applying the bar from step 2.3 therefore gives exactly the triangular expansions in (3), with top coefficient one and all lower coefficients in $A$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 Parts (1), (2), (3) and (4) are proved in steps 1.1, 2.1 together with 2.2, 2.3 together with 3.1, and 2.2 respectively. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1] ∎

items.title: The facet tensor-weight exclusion lemma
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda$ be an integral dot-antidominant dot-regular weight and let $\mu$ be an integral dot-antidominant weight such that the facet $F_\mu$ lies in the closure of the chamber $F_\lambda$, i.e. $\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$ for the positive roots $\alpha\in\Phi_J^+$ of the parabolic subsystem $\Phi_J$ of $J=J(\mu)$ defined in [[def-singular-integral-category-o-block-and-stabilizer]], and $\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle$ has the same sign as $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle$ for every remaining positive root. Let $\nu$ be the unique dominant weight of the linear orbit $W(\mu-\lambda)$ ([[lem-finite-weyl-closed-chambers-and-stabilizers]]) and let $E=L(\nu)$ ([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]]). Then for all $w,w'\in W$ and every weight $\gamma$ of $E$: if $w'\cdot\mu=w\cdot\lambda+\gamma$, then $w'\cdot\mu=w\cdot\mu$ and $\gamma=w(\mu-\lambda)$. Consequently, for every $w$ the tensor $E\otimes\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ has exactly one Verma factor whose central character is that of $\mu$, namely $\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$, and its multiplicity in the Verma flag computed by [[lem-tensoring-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-preserves-verma-flags]] is one.
items.strategy: The proof is the published single-wall proof of [[lem-single-wall-tensor-weight-exclusion]] with the stabilizer $\{1,s\}$ replaced by the full dot stabilizer $W_J$; only the last step changes. Write $\lambda_\bullet=\lambda+\rho$, $\mu_\bullet=\mu+\rho$. From $w'\cdot\mu=w\cdot\lambda+\gamma$ one gets $(w')^{-1}\gamma=\mu_\bullet-x\lambda_\bullet$ with $x=(w')^{-1}w$; the norm bound $|\gamma|\le|\nu|=|\mu_\bullet-\lambda_\bullet|$ ([[lem-weight-norm-bound-for-finite-dimensional-simple-modules]]) and the dominant distance comparison for the dominant vectors $-\mu_\bullet,-\lambda_\bullet$ ([[lem-dominant-norm-distance-comparison]]) give equality throughout; the equality case gives $x(-\lambda_\bullet)\in \operatorname{Stab}_W(-\mu_\bullet)(-\lambda_\bullet)=W_J\,(-\lambda_\bullet)$, so $x\lambda_\bullet\in W_J\lambda_\bullet$, and since $\lambda_\bullet$ is regular, $x\in W_J$. Hence $x\cdot\mu=\mu$ (because $W_J$ is the dot stabilizer) and $w'\cdot\mu=w\cdot\mu$, and $\gamma=w(\mu-\lambda)$; the multiplicity-one clause is [[lem-weight-norm-bound-for-finite-dimensional-simple-modules]]. The central-character clause uses [[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]. The Choice assumption is inherited from the published translation and norm items; no new choice principle is used.

items.title: Parabolic category O for a standard parabolic
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
published category-$\mathcal O$ theory. Let
$\mathfrak p=\mathfrak p_J=\mathfrak l_J\oplus\mathfrak u_J$ be the standard
parabolic of
[[def-standard-parabolic-and-levi-subalgebras-from-simple-roots]], with
reductive parabolic Levi $\mathfrak l_J$, nilradical $\mathfrak u_J$ and Weyl
group $W_J$; the ambient category is $\mathcal O$ of [[def-bgg-category-o]]
with standard objects the Verma modules [[def-verma-module]].

**(1) Dominance for the Levi.** A weight $\lambda$ is **$\mathfrak p$-dominant**
if $\langle\lambda,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ for all
$\alpha\in\Phi_J^+$ (this is dominance for the Levi root system; in particular
$\lambda$ is integral for $\Phi_J$; see
[[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]] for the ambient
notion).

**(2) Generalized Verma modules.** For a $\mathfrak p$-dominant $\lambda$ let
$E(\lambda)$ be the finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak p$-module obtained
from the finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak l_J$-module of highest weight
$\lambda$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]])
by letting $\mathfrak u_J$ act by zero. Define the **generalized Verma module**

$$M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak p)}E(\lambda).$$

**(3) The parabolic category.** The **parabolic category** $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$
is the full subcategory of $\mathcal O$ whose objects are the finitely
generated $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-modules on which
$U(\mathfrak p)$ acts locally finitely, that is, on which every vector lies
in a finite-dimensional $\mathfrak p$-submodule; equivalently, every vector
lies in a finite-dimensional
$\mathfrak l_J$-submodule and is annihilated by a power of $\mathfrak u_J$
(local finiteness for the nilpotent $\mathfrak u_J$).

The following structural facts are part of the definition; the arguments are
given in the Remarks.

**(4) Generalized Vermas lie in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$.** For each
$\mathfrak p$-dominant integral $\lambda$, $M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ is an
object of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ with highest weight $\lambda$, and the
natural surjection $M(\lambda)\twoheadrightarrow M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$
exhibits $M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ as the largest quotient of the Verma
module $M(\lambda)$ that lies in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$.

**(5) Simples.** The simple objects of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ are exactly
the simple highest-weight modules $L(\lambda)$ with $\lambda$
$\mathfrak p$-dominant integral
([[thm-simple-objects-of-category-o-are-highest-weight-modules]]).

**(6) Serre property.** $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ is closed under subobjects,
quotients and extensions in $\mathcal O$; in particular it is an abelian
subcategory of $\mathcal O$ stable under finite direct sums.

**(7) Costandard objects.** For $\mathfrak p$-dominant integral $\lambda$ put
$\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):=D M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$, the restricted
dual of [[prop-restricted-duality-is-an-exact-involution-on-category-o]].
These are the **costandard objects** of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$; each is
naturally a submodule of the ordinary dual Verma $D M(\lambda)$. They need not
be quotients of ordinary dual Vermas.
items.strategy:
Finite l_J modules with h-semisimple action split into center-weight spaces and
then finite simple s_J modules by actual Weyl complete reducibility. Its finite
simples E(η) are parametrized by η integral dominant on J; center acts by η|z_J.
Inflate E to p by u=0. PBW gives Δ^J(η)=U(v_J)⊗E(η). Each bounded negative
ζ-degree piece is finite dimensional and Levi-stable; positive u raises ζ-weight
and hence lowers this degree after PBW reordering, annihilating E at degree0.
Thus these finite pieces are p-stable. This proves p-local finiteness directly.
The natural ordinary Verma surjection shows Δ^J belongs to O and has unique
simple head L(η), one-dimensional top, finite length, and only lower factors.

Inside O, p-local finiteness is equivalent to local nilpotence of every f_j,j∈J.
Necessity uses finite h-weight support of a finite p-module. Conversely a cyclic
Levi submodule is an O-module for s_J: finite center weights, h-semisimplicity,
and local n_J^+-finiteness are inherited. Its finite composition series has
integrable simples, which are finite dimensional by the proved highest-weight
classification; hence it is finite dimensional. Then U(p)m=U(l)U(u)m is finite
because U(u)m is finite in O and each of its finitely many generators is Levi-finite.
Local nilpotence passes through subobjects, quotients and extensions, proving
Serre closure. This proof does not assume extensions of local-finite modules
are automatically local finite for an arbitrary algebra.

A simple highest weight lies in O^p iff its highest weight is J-dominant integral:
necessity is finite Levi highest-weight classification; sufficiency is its quotient
of Δ^J. In any p-finite quotient of Δ(η), the highest vector generates the finite
Levi simple E(η), and u kills it and its Levi span. The induced universal property
forces factorization through Δ^J(η). This is the largest p-finite quotient.
Restricted duality preserves O^p: a locally finite semisimple Levi representation
with finite h-weight spaces is an algebraic direct sum of finite Levi simples
(using an increasing sequence of finite Levi submodules and finite complete reducibility); PBW and finitely many g-generators give a countable spanning list. Its successive finite Levi spans exhaust M; finite complete reducibility splits each inclusion, giving the stated direct sum without importing an infinite semisimplicity theorem. Every weight meets only finitely many summands by finite weight dimension, so its restricted dual is the direct sum of the finite restricted duals. Thus ∇^J(η)=DΔ^J(η) is p-finite and its simple socle is L(η).
It is a submodule of ordinary DΔ(η), not generally a quotient.

items.title: Existence and uniqueness of the parabolic Kazhdan–Lusztig bases
items.statement:
Retain the notation of
[[def-parabolic-hecke-module-and-antispherical-standard-basis]] and
[[lem-the-parabolic-hecke-modules-have-standard-bases-actions-and-compatible-bars]].
For every $x\in{}^JW$ there is a unique $C_x\in M^J$ and a unique
$D_x\in N^J$ with (i) $\overline{C_x}=C_x$ and $\overline{D_x}=D_x$, and (ii)
$C_x\in m_x+\sum_{y<x}v\mathbb Z[v]\,m_y$ and
$D_x\in n_x+\sum_{y<x}v\mathbb Z[v]\,n_y$, the sums over the lower Bruhat
ideal of $x$ inside ${}^JW$. The sets $\{C_x\}_{x\in{}^JW}$ and
$\{D_x\}_{x\in{}^JW}$ are $A$-bases of $M^J$ and $N^J$. No coefficientwise
positivity is asserted.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct: run the triangular bar-fixed induction of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]] over the finite lower Bruhat ideal inside ${}^JW$, for the two modules simultaneously.

1.1 **The coefficient matrices.** Define $r_{x,y}\in A$ for $x,y\in{}^JW$ by $\overline{m_y}=\sum_{x\le y}r_{x,y}m_x$, so $r_{x,y}=a_{x,y}$ for $x<y$, $r_{y,y}=1$, and $r_{x,y}=0$ when $x\not\le y$; define $s_{x,y}$ analogously from $\overline{n_y}=\sum_{x\le y}s_{x,y}n_x$. Applying bar to $\overline{m_y}=\sum_{x\le y}r_{x,y}m_x$ and using $\overline{\overline{m_y}}=m_y$ gives $m_y=\sum_{x\le y}\overline{r_{x,y}}\,\overline{m_x}=\sum_{x'\le y}\bigl(\sum_{x:x'\le x\le y}\overline{r_{x,y}}r_{x',x}\bigr)m_{x'}$; by [F1] the coefficient of $m_{x'}$ is $\delta_{x',y}$, that is, $R\bar R=I$ for the unitriangular matrix $R=(r_{x,y})$. A finite unitriangular matrix is invertible, so also $\bar RR=I$; the same identities hold for $S=(s_{x,y})$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 **Construction of the coefficients.** Fix $w\in{}^JW$ and increase $d=\ell(w)-\ell(x)$ over the finite lower ideal $I_w=\{x\in{}^JW:x\le w\}$ of [F3], starting with $c_{w,w}=1$. Suppose $x<w$ and $c_{y,w}$ has been constructed for every $y\in I_w$ with $x<y\le w$, satisfying $c_{y,w}=\sum_{y\le z\le w}r_{y,z}\overline{c_{z,w}}$; note that all cited labels lie in $I_w$. Put $a_x:=\sum_{x<y\le w}r_{x,y}\overline{c_{y,w}}$. Then $\overline{a_x}=\sum_{x<y\le w}\overline{r_{x,y}}c_{y,w}=\sum_{x<y\le z\le w}\overline{r_{x,y}}r_{y,z}\overline{c_{z,w}}=-\sum_{x<z\le w}r_{x,z}\overline{c_{z,w}}=-a_x$, where the middle equality substitutes the induction equations and the third uses $\bar RR=I$ from step 1.1: the sum over $x\le y\le z$ is zero for $x<z$, and its omitted diagonal term is $\overline{r_{x,x}}r_{x,z}=r_{x,z}$. Write $a_x=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}\gamma_mv^m$; anti-invariance under $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ gives $\gamma_{-m}=-\gamma_m$, hence $\gamma_0=0$. Define $c_{x,w}:=\sum_{m>0}\gamma_mv^m$, so $c_{x,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ and $c_{x,w}-\overline{c_{x,w}}=a_x$. The induction is finite and uses no choice principle. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 **Bar invariance and the coefficient equations.** Set $C_w:=\sum_{y\in I_w}c_{y,w}m_y$. The coefficient of $m_x$ in $\overline{C_w}$ is $\sum_{x\le y\le w}r_{x,y}\overline{c_{y,w}}$. For $x=w$ this is $\overline{c_{w,w}}=1=c_{w,w}$; for $x<w$ it is $\overline{c_{x,w}}+a_x=c_{x,w}$ by step 2.1, and for $x\notin I_w$ the support of $r_{x,y}$ makes the coefficient zero ($x\le y\le w$ would put $x\in I_w$). Hence $\overline{C_w}=C_w$ and the coefficient equation $c_{x,w}=\sum_{x\le y\le w}r_{x,y}\overline{c_{y,w}}$ holds for every $x\le w\in{}^JW$; this proves the existence, the bar invariance and the triangular support $C_w\in m_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]m_y$ of (i),(ii). Repeating the identical construction with the matrix $S$ in place of $R$ produces $D_w\in n_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]n_y$ with $\overline{D_w}=D_w$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 **Uniqueness.** Suppose $h=\sum_{y<w}c_ym_y\in M^J$ is bar-fixed with every $c_y\in v\mathbb Z[v]$. If $h\ne0$, choose a Bruhat-maximal $x$ in its finite support $I_w\setminus\{w\}$. The coefficient of $m_x$ in $\overline h$ is $\overline{c_x}$: no $y>x$ is supported, and $r_{x,y}\ne0$ requires $x\le y$. Since $h=\overline h$ and the $m_y$ are independent, $c_x=\overline{c_x}$; but bar maps $v\mathbb Z[v]$ into $v^{-1}\mathbb Z[v^{-1}]$, so the common value lies in $v\mathbb Z[v]\cap v^{-1}\mathbb Z[v^{-1}]=\{0\}$ by [F4], a contradiction. Hence $h=0$: the bar-fixed element with the prescribed triangular support is unique, and likewise in $N^J$. [F1, F4, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 **Bases.** The transition from $(m_x)_{x\in{}^JW}$ to $(C_x)_{x\in{}^JW}$ is unitriangular over the finite Bruhat order (each $C_x=m_x+\sum_{y<x}c_{y,x}m_y$), so it is invertible over $A$; hence $\{C_x\}$ is an $A$-basis of $M^J$. The same holds for $\{D_x\}$ in $N^J$. This proves the theorem for both modules. [F1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Translation to the wall on Verma, simple and projective objects
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(\lambda,\mu)$ be as
in [[lem-facet-tensor-weight-exclusion]]: $\lambda$ integral dot-antidominant
and dot-regular, $\mu$ integral dot-antidominant with $F_\mu$ in the closure
of the chamber $F_\lambda$, $J=J(\mu)$, $W_\mu=W_J$. Let $\nu$ be the unique
dominant weight of $W(\mu-\lambda)$ and let
$$T:=T_\lambda^\mu=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\mu}\circ(L(\nu)\otimes-)\circ\operatorname{incl}_{\chi_\lambda}\colon\mathcal O_\lambda\longrightarrow\mathcal O_\mu,\qquad T':=T_\mu^\lambda,$$
be the translation functors of [[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]],
which are exact and biadjoint
([[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]]). Then:

**(1)** $T\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\cong\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$ and
$T\nabla(w\cdot\lambda)\cong\nabla(w\cdot\mu)$ for every $w\in W$.

**(2)** $TL(w\cdot\lambda)\cong L(w\cdot\mu)$ if $w\in W^J$, and
$TL(w\cdot\lambda)=0$ otherwise; equivalently $TL(w\cdot\lambda)\neq0$ if and
only if $w$ lies in the set $W^J$ of minimal representatives of the cosets $wW_J$.

**(3) (Big projective on the wall.)** Let
$\Xi_\mu:=T_{-\rho}^{\mu}L(-\rho)$ be the translate of the simple object of
the most singular block. Then $\Xi_\mu$ is projective and injective in
$\mathcal O_\mu$, it is the projective cover $P(1\cdot\mu)$ of $L(\mu)$, and
$(\Xi_\mu:\Delta(w\cdot\mu))=1$ for every distinct orbit label (equivalently
for its representatives $w\in W^J$); consequently
$(P(\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))=1$ for every distinct label $y\in W^J$ and
$[\Delta(w\cdot\mu):L(\mu)]=1$ for all $w\in W$.
items.strategy:
Facet weight exclusion gives TΔ_w=Δ'_w. Finite-dimensional restricted duality fixes E, and finite tensor/weight duality gives D(E tensor M)=E tensor DM; generalized central blocks are dual-stable. Thus restricted-duality compatibility gives
T∇_w=∇'_w. Exactness gives Δ'_w→TL_w→∇'_w. If TL_w is nonzero, its image is
nonzero in the one-dimensional Hom(Δ'_w,∇'_w) and is the simple L'_w. For a
nonminimal w in W/W_J, a proper Verma embedding Δ_{ws}→Δ_w with ws<w,
s∈J, translates to a nonzero map between identical Vermas, hence an isomorphism;
nonzero follows by exactness preserving this injection. Therefore TL_w=0. A
composition series of Δ_w for minimal w must account for L'_w; among its coset
only this minimal w can survive, so TL_w=L'_w. This proves the exact survival
matrix, without claiming every quotient of a simple-head Verma is simple.

The most-singular Δ(-ρ)=L(-ρ) is projective by its top-weight functor and is
injective by duality; its one-simple block is semisimple. Translate it to the
antidominant singular μ using E highest w0(μ+ρ). Norm/extremal weights give one
standard for each DISTINCT orbit label, once. The translate Q is projective-injective.
Reverse adjunction computes Hom(Q,L(μ))=1: E* has highest weight -(μ+ρ), which
is the sole weight giving the projected most-singular Verma in E*Δ(μ).
Thus P(μ) occurs in Q. Every singular Δ(y·μ) contains the simple Δ(μ) by the BGG
embedding criterion; reciprocity forces every standard in P(μ) at least once.
The Q flag has each once, so Q=P(μ) and all these multiplicities are1. Other
projectives need not contain all standards; the native universal ≥1 clause is false.

items.title: Parabolic category O is a highest weight category
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let
$\mathfrak p=\mathfrak l_J\oplus\mathfrak u_J$ and $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$
be as in [[def-parabolic-category-o-for-a-standard-parabolic]]. Then:

**(1) (Simples.)** Within an integral block, $L(\lambda)\in\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$
if and only if $\lambda$ is $\mathfrak p$-dominant integral; every simple
object of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ is of this form.

**(2) (Standards.)** For $\mathfrak p$-dominant integral $\lambda$ the
generalized Verma $M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ lies in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$,
has finite length, has $L(\lambda)$ as its unique simple quotient (head), and
$[M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):L(\mu)]\neq0$ forces $\mu\le\lambda$ in the
dominance order; $M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ is the largest quotient of
$M(\lambda)$ lying in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$.

**(3) (Enough projectives.)** The inclusion
$\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}\subseteq\mathcal O$ is exact and has a left adjoint
$L_{\mathfrak p}$ (the largest $\mathfrak p$-locally-finite quotient);
$L_{\mathfrak p}$ is right exact and sends projective objects of $\mathcal O$
to projective objects of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$. Consequently, for every
$\mathfrak p$-dominant integral $\lambda$ the object
$P^{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):=L_{\mathfrak p}(P^{(\mathcal O)}(\lambda))$ is a
projective cover of $L(\lambda)$ in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$, and
$\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ has enough projectives and injectives.

**(4) (Generalized-standard flags, BGG reciprocity and duality.)** Every
projective in a fixed integral block has a finite generalized Verma flag. Its
projective cover surjects to its labelled generalized standard with a kernel
filtered by higher-labelled generalized standards. The simple and
generalized-standard classes form bases of the finite block Grothendieck
group, and characters are injective on this group. For $\mathfrak p$-dominant
integral $\lambda,\mu$,
$$(P^{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):M_{\mathfrak p}(\mu))=[M_{\mathfrak p}(\mu):L(\lambda)],$$
the multiplicities being finite; moreover restricted duality restricts to an
exact contravariant involution of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ exchanging
$M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ and $\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$, and
$\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}}(M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda),\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\mu))=0$
for all $\lambda,\mu$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **Simples and standards.** By [F1], Levi-dominant integral highest weights are exactly the simple labels in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$. Their generalized standards are quotients of the ordinary Vermas with the same one-dimensional highest-weight space and simple head. They have finite length by [F2], and their weights, and hence highest weights of composition factors, lie in $\lambda-Q^+$ by [F3]. For any parabolic quotient of the ordinary Verma, the image of its highest vector is killed by the full positive nilpotent algebra. Its finite Levi span is the cyclic highest-weight simple $E(\lambda)$ by complete reducibility, and the radical kills that span since it kills the highest vector and is Levi-stable. The induction universal property therefore factors the quotient map through $\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$. This proves the largest-quotient assertion locally. This proves parts (1) and (2). [F1, F2, F3, F4]

1.2 **Largest locally finite quotient.** For $M\in\mathcal O$, let $\mathcal K$ be the set of its subobjects $K$ such that $M/K\in\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$. It contains $M$, and finite length bounds $\ell(M/K)$, so choose $K_0$ for which this quotient length is maximal. For every $K\in\mathcal K$, the diagonal map embeds $M/(K\cap K_0)$ in $M/K\oplus M/K_0$. Serre closure gives $K\cap K_0\in\mathcal K$. Maximality and the epimorphism $M/(K\cap K_0)\to M/K_0$ force equality of lengths; its kernel is therefore zero and $K_0\subseteq K$. Thus $K_0$ is the least kernel among all parabolic quotients. For a map $M\to V$ with $V$ parabolic, its image is parabolic and its kernel lies in $\mathcal K$, so the map factors uniquely through $M/K_0$. This proves the functorial universal property of $L_{\mathfrak p}M=M/K_0$ and its left adjunction to the exact inclusion. It is right exact as a left adjoint. [F1, F2, F6, algebra]

1.3 **The correct Hom arrows.** The ordinary Verma surjection is $M(\eta)\twoheadrightarrow\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\eta)$, and the costandard inclusion is $\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\xi)\hookrightarrow DM(\xi)$. Composing with these maps injects parabolic $\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\eta),\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\xi))$ into the ordinary standard-costandard Hom of [F3]. Thus it is zero for different labels and at most one-dimensional for equal labels. In the equal case the nonzero composite through $L(\eta)$ is a homomorphism from the standard head to the costandard socle, so its dimension is one. [F1, F3, F6, algebra]

1.4 **Every parabolic standard-costandard extension splits.** Consider $0\to\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\xi)\to X\to\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\eta)\to0$. First suppose $\xi-\eta\notin Q^+\setminus\{0\}$, including equality and incomparability. Choose a weight-$\eta$ lift $v$ of the source highest vector. If a positive root vector sent $v$ nontrivially to weight $\eta+\alpha$, its image in the standard quotient would be zero, so this weight would occur in the costandard. But all costandard weights are $\le\xi$; hence $\eta<\eta+\alpha\le\xi$ would imply $\eta<\xi$, contrary to the case assumption. Thus $v$ is killed by every positive root vector. Its Levi span is finite dimensional because $X$ is locally parabolic-finite. By [F4] it is the cyclic finite Levi highest-weight simple $E(\eta)$: complete reducibility decomposes the span, and the nonzero components of a highest-weight vector of weight $\eta$ belong to copies of that same simple, with cyclic diagonal span one copy. The radical kills this whole span since it kills $v$ and $[\mathfrak l,\mathfrak u]\subseteq\mathfrak u$. Induction therefore gives a map $\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\eta)\to X$ whose composite onto the quotient is the identity on its generating top, hence the identity. The extension splits. In the remaining case $\eta<\xi$, duality gives an extension with reversed pair $(\xi,\eta)$, to which the first case applies; dualizing the splitting back finishes the proof. Consequently parabolic $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\eta),\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\xi))=0$ for every pair, proved inside this category. The argument uses the absence of a weight obtained by raising the chosen top, not a total ordering of incomparable highest weights. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, algebra]

1.5 **Finite bounded projectives in an integral summand.** Fix such a central-character summand $\chi$, with dot-dominant $\kappa$ from [F5]. Every weight of every object in it is $\le\kappa$, because its composition factors have highest labels in that dot orbit. The grading element has nonnegative value on $Q^+$, so every $\zeta$-weight is at most $\kappa(\zeta)$. For a parabolic label $\eta$ put $d=\kappa(\zeta)-\eta(\zeta)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ and let $E=E(\eta)$. Define the finite-dimensional $\mathfrak p$-module $B_{\le d}(E)$ by inducing $E$ from the Levi to $\mathfrak p$ and quotienting by all positive-radical PBW terms of $\zeta$-degree greater than $d$. These terms form a submodule since the Levi preserves degree and the radical increases it. On every object $W$ in the summand, a Levi map $E\to W$ automatically kills the excluded terms after extension to $U(\mathfrak p)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak l)}E$, as their weights exceed the bound. The descending radical-degree filtration of this finite module has semisimple Levi slices killed by the radical; exact PBW induction gives a finite generalized-standard flag and places its induction in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ before central projection. Thus $Q(E)=\operatorname{pr}_\chi(U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_B B_{\le d}(E))$ represents $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak l}(E,W)$. This functor is exact: lift a basis of any finite Levi image through an epimorphism, take the finite sum of the Levi spans of those lifts, and split the resulting finite Levi epimorphism by [F4]. Hence $Q(E)$ is projective in this summand and maps onto $L(\eta)$. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 **Projective covers and enough projectives.** The adjunction gives $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}}(L_{\mathfrak p}P,-)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(P,-)$ on the parabolic subcategory, so an ordinary projective has parabolic projective image. For a parabolic simple $L(\lambda)$, apply $L_{\mathfrak p}$ to the ordinary projective cover to obtain $L_{\mathfrak p}P^{(\mathcal O)}(\lambda)\twoheadrightarrow L(\lambda)$. If a subobject of this image surjects onto the simple, its inverse image in the ordinary cover does also and is the whole cover by essentiality. Hence the image map is essential and is the required parabolic projective cover. An ordinary projective epimorphism onto any parabolic object becomes a parabolic projective epimorphism by right exactness. Dualizing gives enough injectives. This proves part (3) on all the objects in the stated parabolic category. [F1, F2, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 **These projectives begin with actual PBW flags.** Filter $B_{\le d}(E)$ by descending radical degree. Each degree slice is finite-dimensional and semisimple for the Levi, with radical acting by zero on the slice. PBW makes induction from $B$ exact, so inducing this filtration gives a finite generalized-standard flag on $U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_B B_{\le d}(E)$. A generalized standard has scalar central character, because its ordinary Verma precursor does; exact central projection therefore either retains or kills each whole standard slice. Hence $Q(E)$ has an actual finite generalized-standard flag. As an $N$-module the unprojected induction is graded free of finite rank, with basis the finite graded space $B_{\le d}(E)$. Central projection is an $N$-linear grading-preserving direct-summand projection. Every parabolic projective cover in the chosen summand is a grading-preserving summand of the corresponding $Q(E)$: lift the epimorphism $Q(E)\to L(\eta)$ to its cover, use essentiality for surjectivity, then split by projectivity. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 1.5, algebra]

4.1 **Graded direct summands stay free.** For a graded $N$-module bounded above, the equality $V=N_{<0}V$ forces $V=0$: a nonzero homogeneous component of highest occupied degree cannot be obtained from strictly higher-degree components. Let $R$ be a grading-preserving direct summand of a finite graded free $N$-module. Then $R/N_{<0}R$ is finite dimensional. Choose a homogeneous basis of this quotient and lifts to $R$, giving a map from a finite graded free module $G$ onto $R$; its cokernel is bounded above and equals its own $N_{<0}$ multiple, so the map is surjective by the preceding argument. It splits as a graded $N$-map since $R$ is a graded projective summand. The kernel $K$ then has $K/N_{<0}K=0$, because the induced map on generator quotients is an isomorphism and reduction of the split sequence is split exact. The same bounded-above argument gives $K=0$. Thus $R$ is graded free of finite rank. This proves the summand claim without importing the flag criterion or assuming finite-dimensional degree-zero pieces of an enveloping Levi algebra. [F4, F6, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 **Free finite rank gives generalized-standard flags.** Let $R$ be one of these parabolic $\mathfrak g$-modules, graded free of finite $N$-rank. Within its fixed $\zeta$-eigenvalue coset its degrees are bounded above and its components finite dimensional. Let $a$ be its highest occupied degree. The finite Levi module $R_a$ is semisimple and the positive radical kills it, as it raises degree. A homogeneous free basis shows that all its degree-$a$ basis vectors are part of an $N$-basis, so the induction map $U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_B R_a=N\otimes R_a\to R$ is injective and its quotient is again graded free, with those finitely many generators removed. Decomposing $R_a$ into finite Levi simples gives an actual submodule that is a finite sum of generalized standards. Repeating on the quotient terminates since each step reduces the finite $N$-rank. All subobjects and quotients lie in the selected central summand; hence their simple Levi labels are the allowed labels there. This proves that every projective cover, and therefore every finite sum and summand of them, has a finite generalized-standard flag. The grading is only the actual semisimple $\zeta$-action, shifted on its coset; it is not a Koszul assumption. This proves the flag part of (4). [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 3.1, step 4.1, induction]

6.1 **Reciprocity.** For a generalized-standard flag of $P^{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$, steps 1.3 and 1.4 make $\operatorname{Hom}(-,\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\mu))$ exact along its flag sequences and show that its dimension counts precisely the $\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\mu)$ sections. On the other hand projectivity makes $\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\mathfrak p}(\lambda),-)$ exact along a composition series of $\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\mu)$. Its value on a simple has dimension one for $L(\lambda)$ and zero for every other label, by the essential simple head of the projective cover. Consequently $(P^{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\mu))=[\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\mu):L(\lambda)]=[\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\mu):L(\lambda)]$, the last equality by simple-preserving duality. This also proves independence of flag multiplicities and their finiteness. By standard support, only $\mu\ge\lambda$ occurs, and the diagonal multiplicity is one. [F1, F2, F6, step 2.1, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 **Labelled standard quotient and its higher-standard kernel.** The same lifting argument as in step 1.4, with $\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\beta)$ in place of the costandard, shows $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\alpha),\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\beta))=0$ whenever $\alpha\not<\beta$: its submodule has no weight strictly above the lifted top $\alpha$, and finite Levi splitting supplies the section. In the flag of $P^{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ from step 5.1, the labelled standard occurs once and every other standard has strictly higher label by step 6.1. Whenever the labelled standard precedes a higher standard in the flag, the corresponding two-section subquotient splits by this Ext vanishing. Swapping those two sections moves the labelled standard upwards in the flag; finitely many swaps place it last. Thus there is an actual epimorphism $P^{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)\to\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ with a kernel having a finite flag of strictly higher standards. This is the highest-weight projective-kernel axiom, obtained without the tilting or homological-criterion suppliers. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.4, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 **Bases, characters and conclusion.** In the fixed integral summand there are finitely many allowed labels by [F5]. Their simple classes form its finite-length Grothendieck basis; the standard-to-simple matrix has diagonal one and entries only below the diagonal after a linear extension of the root order. It is therefore invertible over $\mathbb Z$, so standard classes give another basis. A finite relation between the simple characters has a maximal highest-weight label with a nonzero coefficient; its highest-weight monomial occurs in that simple with coefficient one and in no remaining incomparable or lower simple, so the relation cannot vanish. Inducting proves that characters are injective on this Grothendieck group. The constructions above establish the simples and standard support, the reflector and enough projectives, the local Hom/Ext orthogonality, actual generalized-standard flags, reciprocity and the labelled higher-standard kernel. Duality has remained the ordinary restricted duality restricted to the actual parabolic subcategory. These are all four parts of the Statement. [F1, F2, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1] ∎

items.title: The parabolic Kazhdan–Lusztig bases and polynomials
items.statement:
Retain the notation of
[[def-parabolic-hecke-module-and-antispherical-standard-basis]] and write the
parabolic Kazhdan--Lusztig bases of
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-parabolic-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]] as

$$C_x=\sum_{y\le x,\ y\in{}^JW}m_{y,x}\,m_y,\qquad D_x=\sum_{y\le x,\ y\in{}^JW}n_{y,x}\,n_y,\qquad x\in{}^JW,$$

with coefficients $m_{y,x},n_{y,x}\in\mathbb Z[v]$ supported on the lower
Bruhat ideal, $m_{x,x}=n_{x,x}=1$ and $m_{y,x},n_{y,x}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for
$y<x$.

The **spherical parabolic Kazhdan--Lusztig polynomials** are
$$M^J_{y,x}(q):=v^{-\ell(x)+\ell(y)}m_{y,x},\qquad q=v^{-2},$$
and the **antispherical (sign) parabolic Kazhdan--Lusztig polynomials** are
$$N^J_{y,x}(q):=v^{-\ell(x)+\ell(y)}n_{y,x}.$$
The parity and degree bounds established in
[[thm-parabolic-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-are-alternating-sums-of-ordinary-ones]]
make these polynomials in $q$; that reduction theorem discharges the
well-definedness asserted here and is recorded in `justified_by`. Values at
$v=1$ are written $m_{y,x}(1)$, $n_{y,x}(1)$.

**Normalization dictionary.** With $P^J_{y,x}(u)$ the parabolic polynomials of
Deodhar (1987) attached to the subset $J$, one has
$M^J_{y,x}=P^J_{y^{-1},x^{-1}}$ for $u=-1$ and $N^J_{y,x}=P^J_{y^{-1},x^{-1}}$
for $u=q$, in the index convention of Deodhar and of the anti-spherical
category. Thus the spherical family is the $u=-1$ normalization and the
antispherical family the $u=q$ normalization; the two are not related by a
unit.

**Spherical reduction to ordinary coefficients.** If $W_J$ is finite with
longest element $w_0^J$, then
$$m_{y,x}=p_{w_0^Jy,\,w_0^Jx}\qquad\text{for all }y,x\in{}^JW,$$
where $p$ is the coefficient of the ordinary Kazhdan--Lusztig basis of
[[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]] and
$\underline H_{w}=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ in the normalization of
[[def-normalized-type-a-hecke-algebra-and-its-bar-involution]].
items.strategy: Define m,n as the canonical-basis coefficients already constructed. Their support/diagonal and vZ[v] properties are supplied by the basis theorem. The shifted q-polynomials and the displayed spherical reduction are forward well-definedness claims discharged by the following reduction theorem, declared in justified_by: that proof uses only these m,n coefficients and induced modules, not a presupposed q-polynomial property. Spherical coefficients are ordinary p_{wJ y,wJ x}; antispherical coefficients are sums (-v)^ell(u) p_{uy,x}, with ell(uy)=ell(u)+ell(y). Ordinary coefficient parity and maximal v-degree ell(x)-ell(y) therefore give the corresponding parity and degree bound for both families. Multiplying by v^(ell(y)-ell(x)) leaves only nonpositive even exponents, so it is a polynomial in q=v^-2. The stated Deodhar u=-1 versus u=q dictionary matches Libedinsky–Williamson §2.6; spherical is trivial-character induction and antispherical is sign-character induction. No nonexistent parity clause of the previous existence theorem is cited.

items.title: Parabolic Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials are alternating sums of ordinary ones
items.statement:
Retain the notation of
[[def-parabolic-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-and-polynomials]].

**(1) (Antispherical alternating sum.)** For all $x,y\in{}^JW$,
$$n_{y,x}=\sum_{z\in W_J}(-1)^{\ell(z)}\,v^{\ell(z)}\,p_{zy,\,x},$$
the sum over all $z\in W_J$ (the product $zy$ taken in $S_n$, and $p_{\cdot,x}$
the ordinary coefficient of the Kazhdan--Lusztig basis of
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]], so the inner
coefficients vanish unless $zy\le x$).

**(2) (Spherical reduction.)** If $W_J$ is finite with longest element
$w_0^J$ then for all $x,y\in{}^JW$,
$$m_{y,x}=p_{w_0^Jy,\ w_0^Jx}.$$

In particular both families are computable from the ordinary Kazhdan--Lusztig
coefficients of $S_n$, with no separate recursion.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** compare the antispherical quotient of an ordinary canonical element and the spherical integral left-eigenmodule with their parabolic canonical bases.

1.1 **The antispherical image.** Let $\Phi:H_v(n)\to N^J=A\otimes_{H_J}H_v(n)$, $\Phi(h):=1\otimes h$. It is $A$-linear and satisfies $\Phi(\bar h)=\overline{\Phi(h)}$ by [F3]. Since $\underline H_x$ is bar-fixed, so is $\Phi(\underline H_x)$; expanding $\underline H_x=\sum_{w\le x}p_{w,x}H_w$ and using the parabolic factorization $w=zy$ with $z\in W_J$, $y\in{}^JW$ and $1\otimes H_w=\varphi_-(H_z)n_y=(-v)^{\ell(z)}n_y$ gives $\Phi(\underline H_x)=\sum_{y\in{}^JW}\bigl(\sum_{z\in W_J}(-v)^{\ell(z)}p_{zy,x}\bigr)n_y$. The top coefficient at $y=x$ is $p_{x,x}=1$ (only $z=1$ contributes, since $zx\le x$ with $z\ne1$ would give $\ell(zx)>\ell(x)$); and for a coefficient at $y\ne x$, every contributing term has $zy\le x$, hence $y\le zy$ by [F5] and $y<x$. For $y<x$, every contributing ordinary coefficient has $zy<x$: equality $zy=x$ would contradict the unique parabolic factorization of the minimal representative $x$. Thus $p_{zy,x}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$, and multiplication by $(-v)^{\ell(z)}$ preserves this property. Hence $\Phi(\underline H_x)$ is bar-fixed in $n_x+\sum_{y<x}v\mathbb Z[v]n_y$, so by uniqueness [F4] it equals $D_x$ and matching coefficients gives (1). [F3, F4, F5, algebra]

1.2 **The integral parabolic eigenline.** Put $L=\ell(w_J)$ and $C_J=\sum_{u\in W_J}v^{L-\ell(u)}H_u$. Pairing $u$ with $su$ where $\ell(su)=\ell(u)+1$, the left multiplication rule gives $H_s(a_uH_u+a_{su}H_{su})=a_{su}H_u+(a_u+(v^{-1}-v)a_{su})H_{su}$. This equals $v^{-1}(a_uH_u+a_{su}H_{su})$ iff $a_{su}=v^{-1}a_u$. Iterating along reduced words proves that the simultaneous left eigenvectors in $H_J$ are exactly $A C_J$: their coefficients satisfy $a_u=v^{-\ell(u)}a_e=v^{L-\ell(u)}a_{w_J}$. The same pairing on the right gives $C_JH_s=v^{-1}C_J$. Bar preserves the left eigen-equations, since conjugating $H_sX=v^{-1}X$ gives $H_s^{-1}\overline X=v\overline X$ and hence $H_s\overline X=v^{-1}\overline X$. By [F1] its triangular standard expansion leaves the coefficient of $H_{w_J}$ in $\overline{C_J}$ equal to one. The integral eigenline calculation therefore forces $\overline{C_J}=C_J$. Every $u\in W_J$ is a reduced subword of a reduced expression for the block-reversing longest permutation $w_J$ (sort a block permutation up to the reverse order by adjacent ascents); thus $u\le w_J$. Consequently $C_J$ has the ordinary canonical triangular form, and [F1] identifies it with $\underline H_{w_J}$. [F1, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 **Well-definedness and degree bounds for the antispherical family.** In the formula of step 1.1, a term with $p_{zy,x}\ne0$ has $zy\le x$ and $\ell(zy)=\ell(z)+\ell(y)$ by [F5], so $p_{zy,x}\in v^{\ell(x)-\ell(zy)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by [F1]; multiplying by $(-v)^{\ell(z)}$ gives a contribution in $v^{\ell(x)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$. Hence $n_{y,x}\in v^{\ell(x)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$, so $N^J_{y,x}(q)=v^{\ell(y)-\ell(x)}n_{y,x}$ lies in $\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]=\mathbb Z[q]$ with $q=v^{-2}$, and $n_{y,x}$ has parity $\ell(x)-\ell(y)$ modulo two. This discharges the well-definedness of the antispherical polynomials. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 **The integral spherical image.** Define $\Theta:M^J\to H_v(n)$ by $\Theta(1\otimes h)=C_Jh$. Step 1.2 proves balancing and bar compatibility. Decompose $H_v(n)=\bigoplus_{y\in{}^JW}H_JH_y$ as in [F3]. An element $X=\sum_yh_yH_y$ satisfies $H_sX=v^{-1}X$ for all $s\in J$ iff each $h_y$ does. The integral eigenline calculation of step 1.2 then gives $h_y=c_yC_J$ with $c_y\in A$. Thus the image of $\Theta$ is exactly this integral eigenmodule, and it is injective: the coefficient of $H_{w_Jy}$ in $C_JH_y=\sum_uv^{L-\ell(u)}H_{uy}$ is one, and no other coset contributes to that standard label. By [F2] in the descent case [F6], $\underline H_{w_Jx}$ lies in this image, with unique preimage $X_x=\sum_yc_ym_y$. [F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 **Triangularity and coefficient comparison.** The disjoint coset expansions in step 2.2 give $c_y=p_{w_Jy,w_Jx}$. The coefficient $c_x$ is one. If $c_y\ne0$, then $w_Jy\le w_Jx$, so $y\le w_Jy\le w_Jx$. Choose a reduced expression for $w_Jx$ consisting of a word in $J$ followed by a reduced expression for $x$. By [F5] it contains a reduced subword for $y$. Such a subword cannot select any letter from the initial $J$-word: its first selected letter would be in $J$, making it a left descent of $y$, contrary to $y\in{}^JW$. Thus the subword lies entirely in $x$, proving $y\le x$. For $y\ne x$, the ordinary coefficient $p_{w_Jy,w_Jx}$ lies in $v\mathbb Z[v]$ by [F1]. Bar compatibility and injectivity give $\overline{X_x}=X_x$. Therefore $X_x$ has exactly the defining canonical form in [F4], so $X_x=C_x$ and $m_{y,x}=p_{w_Jy,w_Jx}$. This proves (2), including zero coefficients outside the lower ideal. [F1, F4, F5, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 **Degree bounds and conclusion.** The ordinary degree bound of [F1] gives $p_{w_0^Jy,w_0^Jx}\in v^{\ell(x)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$, so $m_{y,x}$ has parity $\ell(x)-\ell(y)$ and $M^J_{y,x}(q)=v^{\ell(y)-\ell(x)}m_{y,x}\in\mathbb Z[q]$. Both families are therefore computable from the ordinary coefficients by (1) and (2), and both polynomial families are well defined. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Singular category O multiplicities are parabolic Kazhdan–Lusztig values
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and work in the type-$A$
root datum $W=S_n$ of the page's Hecke module and ordinary multiplicity
theorem. Let $(\lambda,\mu)$ be as in [[lem-facet-tensor-weight-exclusion]]
with $J=J(\mu)$, so $\mathcal O_\mu$ is the singular integral block of
[[def-singular-integral-category-o-block-and-stabilizer]] with labels
normalized by the minimal right coset representatives $W^J$, and let $w_0$ be
the longest element of $W$. Then for all $y,w\in W^J$,
$$[M(y\cdot\mu):L(w\cdot\mu)]=(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))=P_{yw_0,\,ww_0}(1),$$
the value at $q=1$ of the ordinary Kazhdan--Lusztig polynomial attached to the
pair $(yw_0,ww_0)$ in the classical normalization of
[[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]].
Equivalently, put $k(w)=w_0^Jw^{-1}w_0\in{}^JW$. Then
$$[M(y\cdot\mu):L(w\cdot\mu)]=m_{k(y),k(w)}(1).$$
This is the spherical family. The antispherical family instead governs the
genuine regular parabolic locally finite category with dominant labels;
changing to an opposite positive system does not identify the two families.
In particular all singular multiplicities are computable from the ordinary
Kazhdan--Lusztig coefficients of $S_n$, and no individual polynomial
coefficients beyond the value at one occur.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct: push a composition series of the regular standard through the exact translation functor, count only the surviving minimal-representative simple, and translate the labels to the dominant base.

1.1 **Composition multiplicities on the wall.** Fix $y,w\in W^J$ and a composition series of $\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)$ with factors $L(z\cdot\lambda)$, $z\in W$. Exactness of $T$ [F2] turns it into a series of $T\Delta(y\cdot\lambda)\cong\Delta(y\cdot\mu)$ with factors $TL(z\cdot\lambda)$; by [F2] the only nonzero factors occur for $z\in W^J$, and then the factor is $L(z\cdot\mu)$, which can equal the simple $L(w\cdot\mu)$ only for $z=w$ since distinct $W^J$-labels have distinct dot translates [F1]. Hence $[\Delta(y\cdot\mu):L(w\cdot\mu)]=[\Delta(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 **Translate to the dominant base.** Let $\lambda_{\mathrm{dom}}:=w_0\cdot\lambda$; since $\lambda$ is dot-antidominant regular, $\lambda_{\mathrm{dom}}$ is dominant regular and $\lambda=w_0\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{dom}}$, so for every $z\in W$, $z\cdot\lambda=(zw_0)\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{dom}}$. Applying [F3] in the regular block of $\lambda_{\mathrm{dom}}$ gives $[\Delta(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]=[M(yw_0\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{dom}}):L(ww_0\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{dom}})]=P_{yw_0,ww_0}(1)$, the ordinary value supported on $yw_0\le ww_0$. [F3, algebra]

1.3 **The spherical dictionary.** Conjugation by $w_0$ permutes the type-$A$ simple reflections, so the assignment $H_z\mapsto H_{w_0zw_0}$, $v\mapsto v$ is an algebra automorphism: it preserves the quadratic and braid presentations, the bar, length and Bruhat order. It sends a bar-fixed triangular element with top $H_b$ to one with top $H_{w_0bw_0}$; uniqueness in [F4] therefore gives $p_{a,b}=p_{w_0aw_0,w_0bw_0}$. Now set $k(w)=w_0^Jw^{-1}w_0$. Inversion sends $W^J$ to ${}^JW$ [F5]. In type $A$, left-minimality means that the values in each consecutive $J$-block occur in increasing order: the left descent $s_i$ occurs exactly when $i+1$ precedes $i$ in one-line notation. Right multiplication by $w_0$ reverses all positions, making those values decrease; left multiplication by $w_0^J$ reverses the values inside each block, restoring increasing order. Thus $k(w)\in{}^JW$. The spherical reduction [F5] gives $m_{k(y),k(w)}=p_{w_0^Jk(y),w_0^Jk(w)}=p_{y^{-1}w_0,w^{-1}w_0}=p_{w_0y,w_0w}=p_{yw_0,ww_0}$, using simultaneous inversion from [F4] and the conjugation symmetry just proved. Evaluating at $v=1$ and applying the classical normalization yields $m_{k(y),k(w)}(1)=P_{yw_0,ww_0}(1)$. [F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 **The projective version.** By BGG reciprocity [F1], $(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))=[M(y\cdot\mu):L(w\cdot\mu)]=P_{yw_0,ww_0}(1)$; this is the second displayed identity. [F1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 **Conclusion.** Combining the preceding steps, $[M(y\cdot\mu):L(w\cdot\mu)]=(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))=P_{yw_0,ww_0}(1)=m_{k(y),k(w)}(1)$ for all $y,w\in W^J$, so the singular multiplicities are spherical parabolic values at one. The antispherical family is a different family (it is the sign-module normalization, used for the genuine regular parabolic category with dominant labels), and no change of positive system identifies the two; this is exactly the normalization distinction recorded in [[def-parabolic-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-and-polynomials]]. [F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 1.3] ∎

items.title: Parabolic category O multiplicities are parabolic Kazhdan–Lusztig values
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a dominant regular
integral weight $\lambda$ of the complex type-$A$ Lie algebra and the standard
parabolic $\mathfrak p_J$, with reductive Levi $\mathfrak l_J$ and longest
Levi Weyl element $w_J$
([[def-standard-parabolic-and-levi-subalgebras-from-simple-roots]]). The
$\mathfrak p_J$-dominant weights in this regular block are exactly
$y\cdot\lambda$ for $y\in{}^JW$. Write
$\Delta^J(y\cdot\lambda)=M_{\mathfrak p}(y\cdot\lambda)$,
$L(x\cdot\lambda)$ and $P^J(x\cdot\lambda)$ for its generalized standards,
simples and projective covers
([[def-parabolic-category-o-for-a-standard-parabolic]]). Then for
$x,y\in{}^JW$,
$$[\Delta^J(y\cdot\lambda):L(x\cdot\lambda)]=(P^J(x\cdot\lambda):\Delta^J(y\cdot\lambda))=\sum_{u\in W_J}(-1)^{\ell(u)}P_{uy,x}(1)=n_{y,x}(1).$$

These are the antispherical sign coefficients, with support $y\le x$ and
diagonal $1$. The precise character/Grothendieck identity supplying the
formula is
$$\operatorname{ch}\Delta^J(y\cdot\lambda)=\sum_{u\in W_J}(-1)^{\ell(u)}\operatorname{ch}\Delta(uy\cdot\lambda).$$

For the same highest weights in the antidominant base
$\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}}=w_0\cdot\lambda$, the actual longest-left label is
$z=yw_0$, since $y\cdot\lambda=z\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}}$.
Its shortest-left encoding is $a=\mathrm{lf}(y):=w_Jyw_0\in{}^JW$, so the
weight in that encoding is $(w_Ja)\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}}$, not
$a\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}}$. With $b=\mathrm{lf}(x)$, the reindexed matrix is
$$\widetilde N_{a,b}:=n_{\mathrm{lf}^{-1}(a),\mathrm{lf}^{-1}(b)}(1)=n_{w_Jaw_0,\,w_Jbw_0}(1).$$
It is the same multiplicity matrix with both indices permuted and has reversed
support in the transported order. It is not in general $n_{a,b}(1)$.
Every label retains its explicit dot-baseweight.
The highest-weight category theorem applies also to singular integral
parabolic blocks, but this ordinary regular KL matrix formula assumes the
ambient central character is regular. No singular/parabolic category
equivalence, grading or Koszul duality is asserted.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct: prove the finite-Levi character identity, compare ordinary simple coefficients using the regular Kazhdan-Lusztig multiplicity theorem, and read off the antispherical matrix and its projective version.

1.1 **Levi character identity.** Multiply the Weyl character formula [F3] for $E(\xi)$ by the outside PBW denominator of [F2]. For each $u\in W_J$, $u(\rho-\rho_J)=\rho-\rho_J$ by [F3], so $e^{u(\xi+\rho_J)+( \rho-\rho_J)}=e^{u(\xi+\rho)}$; dividing by the full PBW denominator $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(e^{\alpha/2}-e^{-\alpha/2})=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi_J^+}(\ldots)\prod_{\beta\notin\Phi_J^+}(\ldots)$ turns each summand into $\operatorname{ch}\Delta(u\cdot\xi)$ ([[thm-pbw-model-of-a-verma-module]]). Hence, for $\mathfrak p$-dominant integral $\xi$, $\operatorname{ch}\Delta^J(\xi)=\sum_{u\in W_J}(-1)^{\ell(u)}\operatorname{ch}\Delta(u\cdot\xi)$ in the completed character ring; this is the displayed identity at $\xi=y\cdot\lambda$. [F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 **The dominant labels.** Put $A=\lambda+\rho$, strictly dominant and integral. The weight $y\cdot\lambda$ is $\mathfrak p_J$-dominant iff $\langle yA,\alpha_j^\vee\rangle-1\ge0$ for every $j\in J$. The integer $\langle A,y^{-1}\alpha_j^\vee\rangle$ is positive exactly when $y^{-1}\alpha_j$ is a positive root: strict dominance makes positive-root coroot pairings positive integers and negative-root pairings negative. Thus the condition is $y^{-1}\alpha_j>0$ for all $j\in J$, equivalently no LEFT descent $s_jy<y$: in type $A$, $y^{-1}\alpha_j>0$ means that the position of value $j$ precedes that of $j+1$, exactly the inversion-length ascent condition for swapping those values. These are precisely the shortest-left representatives ${}^JW$ in the coset-minimum convention of [F4]; no inversion of the weight label is performed. [F4, algebra]

2.1 **Comparing simple coefficients.** By [F1] the parabolic simples are the $L(x\cdot\lambda)$, $x\in{}^JW$. Taking the coefficient of $L(x\cdot\lambda)$ in the identity of step 1.1 (with $\xi=y\cdot\lambda$, $y\in{}^JW$) and using [F4] and [F5] for the ordinary Vermas in the given dominant regular integral block gives $[\Delta^J(y\cdot\lambda):L(x\cdot\lambda)]=\sum_{u\in W_J}(-1)^{\ell(u)}[M(uy\cdot\lambda):L(x\cdot\lambda)]=\sum_{u\in W_J}(-1)^{\ell(u)}P_{uy,x}(1)=n_{y,x}(1)$. The sum is finite and the coefficients with $uy\not\le x$ vanish; in particular the support is $y\le x$ with diagonal $n_{x,x}(1)=1$. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 **Projective multiplicities.** By the parabolic BGG reciprocity of [F1], $(P^J(x\cdot\lambda):\Delta^J(y\cdot\lambda))=[\Delta^J(y\cdot\lambda):L(x\cdot\lambda)]=n_{y,x}(1)$; the multiplicities are finite by the finite generalized-standard flag of [F1]. This proves the second identity. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 **Native longest-left labels.** Let $\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}}=w_0\cdot\lambda$. Dot-action composition gives $y\cdot\lambda=(yw_0)\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}}$ and $x\cdot\lambda=(xw_0)\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}}$. If $y$ has no left descent in $J$, each $y^{-1}\alpha_j$ is positive, so $(yw_0)^{-1}\alpha_j=w_0y^{-1}\alpha_j$ is negative; hence $z=yw_0$ is the longest representative in its left $W_J$-coset. Its shortest-left encoding is $a=w_Jz=w_Jyw_0$, with inverse $y=w_Jaw_0$; similarly $b=w_Jxw_0$ has inverse $x=w_Jbw_0$. Consequently the same multiplicity of step 2.1 is $[\Delta^J((w_Ja)\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}}):L((w_Jb)\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}})]=n_{w_Jaw_0,w_Jbw_0}(1)=\widetilde N_{a,b}$. This is an honest permutation of rows and columns, with support transported from $w_Jaw_0\le w_Jbw_0$, not a claim that $\widetilde N_{a,b}=n_{a,b}(1)$. Choosing the transported reversed order reads the same matrix as lower triangular. [F1, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The preceding steps prove the multiplicity formula, its projective form, the character identity and the reindexed version; the statement that only the regular ambient central character is assumed, and that no singular/parabolic equivalence or grading is used, is exactly the scope of the quoted suppliers [F1]--[F5]. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

items.title: The parabolic Kazhdan–Lusztig character formula
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and the dominant regular
integral conventions of
[[thm-parabolic-category-o-multiplicities-are-parabolic-kl-polynomials]]. Put
$N=(n_{y,x}(1))_{y,x\in{}^JW}$, with rows indexed by generalized standards and
columns by simples in a Bruhat-compatible order
([[def-parabolic-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-and-polynomials]]). Then $N$ is upper
unitriangular and, for each $x$,
$$\operatorname{ch}L(x\cdot\lambda)=\sum_{y\ge x}(N^{-1})_{x,y}\,\operatorname{ch}\Delta^J(y\cdot\lambda).$$
Its inverse entries are integers computed by the finite signed chain sum of
products of $n_{a,b}(1)$; they are weighted incidence inverses, not generally
ordinary Bruhat Mobius values. In the antidominant base $\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}}=w_0\cdot\lambda$, set
$a=\mathrm{lf}(y)=w_Jyw_0$ and encode the same weight as
$(w_Ja)\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}}$. The reindexed matrix is
$\widetilde N_{a,b}=N_{\mathrm{lf}^{-1}(a),\mathrm{lf}^{-1}(b)}$
and its inverse is reindexed by the same permutation; thus the same formula
has reversed support in the transported order. This does not replace the
entries by $n_{a,b}(1)$.
This is the ungraded
character formula for the regular parabolic block, and constructs no Koszul or
Ext grading.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct finite linear algebra on the unitriangular multiplicity matrix.

1.1 **The matrix equation.** In the Grothendieck group write $M_y:=[\Delta^J(y\cdot\lambda)]$ and $L_x:=[L(x\cdot\lambda)]$; by [F1] and the Jordan-Holder theorem in the finite-length parabolic block, $M_y=\sum_x[\,\Delta^J(y\cdot\lambda):L(x\cdot\lambda)\,]L_x=\sum_{x\ge y}n_{y,x}(1)L_x$. Since the simple classes form a basis by [F2], this is the matrix equation $M=NL$ with $N=(n_{y,x}(1))$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 **Unitriangularity and inversion.** By [F1], $n_{x,x}(1)=1$ and $n_{y,x}(1)=0$ unless $y\le x$; the diagonal of $N$ is one and $U:=N-I$ is strictly upper triangular for the finite Bruhat-compatible order on ${}^JW$. Hence $U$ is nilpotent ($U^{m}=0$ for $m>\#{}^JW$) and $N^{-1}=I-U+U^2-\cdots$ is a finite sum of integer matrices; the $(x,y)$-entry of $N^{-1}$ is supported on $y\ge x$ and equals the finite signed chain sum $\sum_{m\ge0}(-1)^m\sum_{x=z_0<z_1<\cdots<z_m=y}\prod_{i}n_{z_i,z_{i+1}}(1)$ over strictly increasing chains. These are weighted incidence inverses of the finite poset, not generally ordinary Mobius values. [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 **The character formula.** Solving step 1.1 by step 1.2 gives $L=N^{-1}M$ with $N^{-1}$ read as a matrix whose rows are indexed by the simples and whose columns are indexed by the generalized standards, that is, $\operatorname{ch}L(x\cdot\lambda)=\sum_y(N^{-1})_{x,y}\operatorname{ch}\Delta^J(y\cdot\lambda)$; since $(N^{-1})_{x,y}$ is supported on $y\ge x$, this is exactly the displayed formula. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 **Reindexing and conclusion.** Use $a=\mathrm{lf}(y)=w_Jyw_0$ as the shortest-left encoding of the actual longest-left label $yw_0$ in the antidominant base, so the same weight is $(w_Ja)\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}}$. The corrected dictionary in [[thm-parabolic-category-o-multiplicities-are-parabolic-kl-polynomials]] gives $\widetilde N_{a,b}=N_{\mathrm{lf}^{-1}(a),\mathrm{lf}^{-1}(b)}$. Reindexing both coordinates is conjugation by a permutation matrix, hence $\widetilde N^{-1}_{a,b}=N^{-1}_{\mathrm{lf}^{-1}(a),\mathrm{lf}^{-1}(b)}$; therefore $\operatorname{ch}L((w_Ja)\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}})=\sum_b\widetilde N^{-1}_{a,b}\operatorname{ch}\Delta^J((w_Jb)\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{anti}})$, with the original support transported by $\mathrm{lf}$. Choosing the transported reversed order makes this matrix lower triangular. This preserves every character formula and constructs no Koszul or Ext grading. [F1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
